en: The Essential Compendium of the Vinaya Rituals for the Poṣadha Ceremony, Expounding the Characteristics of the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Precepts, by the Śramaṇa Ruxing.

I have heard that when the Great Awakened One first attained enlightenment, he initially formulated the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa; this continued until his final entry into parinirvāṇa at the Twin Śāla Trees.
[The Buddha] entered parinirvāṇa. He also instructed the bhikṣus: "You should always cherish, revere, and respect the Prātimokṣa from beginning to end.

When the Buddha was in the world, he was taken as the teacher; now that we are far removed from the Sage, whom shall we take as our teacher? [The answer is: That which has been taught by the Noble Ones.
To take the precepts as one's teacher—how extraordinary! The precepts are the ladder for ascending to the state of sagehood and the compassionate vessel for crossing the sea of suffering.

Whether monastics or laypeople, once they have entered the ranks of those who uphold the precepts, they should maintain strict protection over their four modes of conduct and ensure the three karmas are perpetually pure.

They should emulate the majestic deportment of Aśvajit and follow the model of Upāli. Whether moving or still, in meditation or reflection, their minds should always remain fixed on the Path. They should constantly delight in solitary seclusion.
He did not associate with laypeople or men of high station. He relied on circumstances for his food and clothing; when he received many offerings, he would discard two and keep one.

Regarding his three robes and ritual implements, he always knew contentment and sufficiency, seeking nothing beyond his needs. Day and night, he single-mindedly cultivated pure practices and the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.

Throughout their lives they remained diligent; their evil karma melted away like ice, and the realm of the Buddha appeared before them. When their hundred-year retribution ended, they were free from all illness and suffering, passing away while sitting upright.
In the place where Amitābha receives and leads sentient beings, one personally receives a prophecy of enlightenment.

Having received this prophecy, one rides upon the wheel of past vows to return to the realm of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*), repaying the four debts of gratitude in their entirety and delivering all beings within the three realms of existence. Thus, the debt to the Buddha can be repaid; this is true renunciation.

To uphold the precepts as foremost—how joyful this is! In this degenerate age (*mofa*), when times have shifted, this Dharma-gate has arisen. How marvelous! It causes the True Dharma to flourish. How extraordinary! May it cause the True [Dharma]...

May the Dharma abide long in the world; may the right faith of sentient beings remain unbroken; may this serve as a model for future generations and establish a great standard for widespread practice.
The verse says:
The three robes draped upon the body transcend the mundane world; All Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are likewise so.
Kāśyapa holds his robe, awaiting Maitreya; Through successive generations, eminent monks have passed it down from patriarch to patriarch.
In the autumn of the Final Dharma, the robe turns white; The True Dharma will not long remain among humans—who can now practice according to the Dharma?
Before departing, he has already transcended the ordinary, though he has not yet attained the fruits of the Path.
The characteristics of the precepts in the Sūtras and Vinaya, along with the ritual procedures for the Poṣadha ceremony, are set forth below.
Regarding the characteristics of the five precepts for upāsakas and upāsikās:
first is the precept against killing; second is the precept against stealing.
The third is the precept against sexual misconduct; the fourth is the precept against false speech;
and the fifth is the precept against drinking alcohol and eating meat.
The Upādhyāya or Ācārya shall examine the transgressions committed by the layman or laywoman, but must not examine them with excessive detail.
Regarding the characteristics of the precepts transgressed during this interval, I shall briefly inquire about killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, so that you may perform repentance.

The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "The eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) for an upāsaka is as follows: 'preventing wrongdoing and ceasing evil' is called *guān* (the barrier/gate); 'not eating after noon' is called *zhāi* (the fast).
If laymen or laywomen receive and maintain these for the duration of their lives, they will certainly attain Bodhi; even receiving them for a single day and night [yields great merit]."
One who observes the eight precepts of the fast surpasses the five precepts for one lifetime. Why does this sudden leap occur? It is because the number of precepts is greater.

To encourage their observance for even half a day, the power of the minor merit of such a fast brings the reward of sixty thousand years of provisions. Yet worldly people mistakenly practice this by choosing only auspicious mornings.
The statement that "one does not drink even water day and night" is an error.
Regarding the characteristics of the eight precepts for upāsakas and upāsikās:
first, abstaining from taking life; second, abstaining from stealing; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct.
Fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to drink alcohol or eat meat;
sixth, not to wear flower garlands, jeweled necklaces, or apply fragrant oils to the body;
seventh, not to go to see or listen to singing, dancing, theatrical performances, or music.
8. Not sitting on high or wide beds; 9. Not eating at improper times—these are the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras:
1. Not killing living beings; 2. Not stealing; 3. Not violating the practice of celibacy.
Fourth, not to engage in false speech; fifth, not to drink alcohol or eat meat;
sixth, not to wear flower garlands, jeweled necklaces, or apply fragrant oils to the body;
seventh, not to engage in singing, dancing, or performing music, nor to go to see or listen to such performances.
8. Not to sit on high, wide, or large beds; 9. Not to eat at improper times;
10. Not to handle raw gold, silver, coins, or treasures.
These are the characteristics of the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu.
The four *pārājika* dharmas, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas,
the two *aniyata* dharmas, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas,
the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas, and the four *prātideśanīya* dharmas.
One hundred rules for training; seven methods for settling disputes;
three hundred and forty-eight rules of discipline for bhikṣuṇīs;
eight pārājika rules; and seventeen saṃghāvaśeṣa rules.
Thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules,
one hundred and seventy-eight *pāyattika* rules, eight *pratideśanīya* rules, one hundred rules for training (*śaikṣa-dharma*),
and seven rules for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
The various schools all lack the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules; they possess only three hundred and forty-eight precepts. These are derived from the four schools.
In the extensive Vinaya, the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya, there are only two hundred and seventy-seven precepts.
When examining the bhikṣuṇī precepts, one must not inquire in detail about specific offenses committed during the interim;
rather, one should briefly question them regarding the four pārājikas and eight saṃghāvaśeṣas, causing them to perform repentance.
The Ritual for Examining Precepts (*Śīla-parīkṣā-vidhi*). Generally, when one receives the precepts, they shall invite a master to stand before the Three Jewels and confess their faults openly.
The administrative officer shall arrange the seats and display incense and flowers. The *Vina* leads the assembly to invite the *Ācārya* who examines the precepts;

holding incense, he is welcomed into the Dharma Hall. After the formal offering of incense and the recitation of praises are completed, the sons of the Buddha each take up incense and perform three prostrations.
Prostrate. Kneel single-mindedly with palms joined.
Once the assembly has finished reciting the Great Compassion Mantra once, chant "Gandhahasti Bodhisattva" three times.
The Upādhyāya has dispatched me to request [Name] Ācārya on your behalf to serve as your *vinayānuśāsaka-ācārya*.
Now, before this teacher’s seat, kneel with your right knee on the ground and join your palms. You must listen attentively to all his instructions.
From the time of birth until now, whatever transgressions of the precepts have been committed, one should disclose them one by one before the Triple Gem and repent openly, without concealment;
for only when a vessel has been thoroughly cleansed can it be filled with nectar.
"O sons of the Buddha, these words of request for a preceptor ought to be spoken by you yourselves; yet fearing that you may not yet be able to do so, you shall all follow my lead:
'Virtuous One, please attend with one-pointed mind. For me, [so-and-so], I now request the Virtuous One to act as the Preceptor for Examining the Precepts (*śīla-parīkṣā-ācārya*) for our assembly.
By relying upon the Virtuous One, I shall be able to perform the method of repentance according to reality. Out of compassion, out of compassion.'"
Out of great compassion, O sons of the Buddha:
since you have made this earnest request, I shall act as your *śīla-viniścaya-ācārya* (preceptor for the examination of precepts).
Listen with single-minded attention to all my instructions. (Strike the sounding block.)

O Sons of the Buddha: from time immemorial until this very day, while we did not yet know the Buddha, had not heard the Dharma, or encountered the Sangha, and were ignorant of good and evil, we committed the deeds of immediate retribution and the three unwholesome physical actions—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
No. There are four unwholesome actions of speech: false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, and divisive speech. There are three unwholesome actions of mind: greed, anger, and wrong view.

Killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, shedding the blood of a Buddha, destroying monasteries, burning scriptures and images, slandering the True Dharma, and becoming an icchantika—all such evils are immeasurable and infinite.
"O you who have reached the limits [of transgression], we now, before the Buddhas of the ten directions, confess our faults and beg for compassion; may you grant that they be extinguished.
This is called the confession of general characteristics. Good sons, as for the confession of specific characteristics, I shall now question you one by one;
you must each answer truthfully. If you do not answer truthfully, you will incur the sin of intentional falsehood."

"Good sons, from the time one is a householder until the time one goes forth, among the four root offenses committed in the past or present, there are those that should be confessed and those that should not be confessed. Good sons, as for those that should not be confessed:
if one has taken human life, stolen the property of the Triple Gem, or committed sexual misconduct with one’s own parents, paternal uncles, or elder sisters."
"Uncle, one who has defiled a bhikṣuṇī of pure conduct should not be granted repentance. As for those who speak great falsehoods:

claiming to have attained what they have not attained, or to have realized what they have not realized; saying that devas come, nāgas come, ghosts come, or spirits come; or that whirlwinds and earth-spirits all arrive at my dwelling."
To manifest wonders to delude the masses, to crave the offerings of others for one’s own livelihood—if one commits such offenses, they are not to be repented.
Son of good family, I now ask you: that which should be repented is as follows. If one kills livestock, repentance is permitted.
To steal another’s property, even a single needle or a single blade of grass—taking what is not given—is all termed theft. To commit sexual misconduct with...
Fellows, you should perform repentance for these things: false speech and frivolous talk; claiming existence when it is empty, and claiming emptiness when it exists;
as well as intentional lying. I pray that these may be extinguished. Good sons, I now ask you again:

from birth to birth, you have consumed wine and meat, deluding the truth and losing your original nature, inciting strife between two families, and failing to recognize the distinction between the honorable and the lowly. For those such as these—
Each and every offense must be individually disclosed and confessed. The vessels must be washed clean before the nectar can be stored within them.
If one does not act in this manner, it is all termed "unlawful" (*adharma*), and according to the Vinaya, such offerings cannot be accepted (each person must complete their individual disclosure).
The Preceptor of Examination should require [the candidate] to undergo arduous prayer, prostrate before a thousand Buddhas, and purify their transgressions; only then may the precepts be received.
All evil karma created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion, Produced through body, speech, and mind— I repent of all these roots of sin.

Examine the śrāmaṇera precepts. Use the same petition as before. Whether the bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs have received the ten śrāmaṇera precepts long ago or recently, they must not have violated the five precepts before receiving the ten precepts.
If there are those who have committed violations, instruct them to perform repentance according to the Dharma so that they become fit to receive the precept-dharmas.
If there are śrāmaṇerīs in the assembly, examine them separately; they must not be examined together with the group. If an examination is unnecessary, [so be it].
Inquire in detail regarding the matters committed during the interim. Briefly examine the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and have them confessed.
Once they have been made to repent according to the Dharma, they may receive the ten precepts.

The Ritual for Examining the Śrāmaṇera Precepts (When a śrāmaṇera receives the bhikṣu precepts, it is also the same as the ritual for the five precepts. The methods of repentance and the wording of the invitation are the same as before. The invocation states:
Upon hearing the sound of the chime, all the śrāmaṇeras prostrate three times, then kneel together in the Hu-style, join their palms, and announce their names.
The Acharya strikes the sounding-block.

A multi-storied tower has four levels, which are ascended one by one in succession. If you wish to ascend the third level of this tower and receive the full and perfect precepts, you must clearly declare each of the characteristics of the ten precepts previously received. If there have been any transgressions, [you must disclose them] as follows:
One must truly confess and repent; one must not conceal faults or hide them within the heart. One should bring these matters before others to repent.
If one does not thus confess and reveal them, the offenses will increase daily, and one will be unfit to receive your precepts.
O śrāmaṇeras, I now ask you according to reality; you must each answer truthfully. O śrāmaṇeras, from the time you received the ten precepts, if...
Regarding precepts violated whether long ago or recently, one must disclose them according to the facts and perform repentance in accordance with the Dharma to purify one's vessel.
Only after performing the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of one motion and three proclamations) before the seated masters may one receive the full Bhikṣu precepts.

If one does not repent according to the facts, advancement to receive the precepts is not permitted; such cases are termed "unlawful" (*adharma*), and the precepts are not obtained. The Precept Master must also ensure that the candidate performs prostrations and repentance.
Purification of Transgressions (the assembly recites the various evil karmas committed in the past).
The ritual for the examination of the śrāmaṇera precepts is concluded; next is the ritual for the examination of the bhikṣu precepts (the invitation is as before).
"Let those who have received the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the ten precepts depart. We shall now examine the bhikṣu precepts.
All you great bhikṣus who now wish to seek the bodhisattva precepts, each with a single mind, take up incense, kneel on your right knees, and join your palms."
The Master on the altar has appointed us to arrange the seats and invite [Name] Ācārya to serve as your *vinayoddeśaka-ācārya*. You bhikṣus, each of you should respectfully extend the invitation;
it is fitting that you state this yourselves. Fearing that you may not yet be able to do so, all of you follow my lead.
Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. I, [Name], and this assembly, seeking the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, desire to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
I now request the Venerable One to serve as my Preceptor for Examining the Precepts (*śīla-parīkṣā-ācārya*). May the Venerable One deign to serve as my Preceptor for Examining the Precepts.
Relying upon the Venerable One, I shall receive the three clusters and ten inexhaustible pure precepts. Out of compassion, [please grant this].
Therefore, out of compassion, out of great compassion, the Preceptor strikes the sounding-block.
O Great Bhikṣus, since you have so earnestly extended this request, I shall act as your Preceptor for the examination of precepts (*śīla-parīkṣā-ācārya*).
Listen with single-minded attention to all my instructions. Now, [Name]...
The Master of the Platform has appointed me to serve as your *vicaya-ācārya* (preceptor for examining the precepts).
I now question you; answer according to the truth and do not harbor false perceptions. If you have committed an offense, say that you have; if you have committed none, say that you have none.

You must not answer falsely. I now ask you: regarding the full ordination (*upasampadā*) you have received, whether it was long ago or recently, there are two hundred and fifty aspects of the precepts (*śīla-lakṣaṇa*).
Ten items: namely, regarding the four *pārājika* dharmas, has there been any transgression? Answer: (Yes/No).
Regarding the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas, has there been any transgression? Answer: (Yes/No).
Regarding the two indeterminate rules (*aniyata-dharma*): has anything been transgressed? Answer: No.
Regarding the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* rules: has anything been transgressed? Answer: No.
"Are there any violations of the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas? Answer: "None.
"Are there any violations of the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas? Answer: "None."
Regarding the one hundred rules of training (*śaikṣa-dharma*): is there anything transgressed? Answer: No.
Regarding the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*): is there anything transgressed? Answer: No.

I now ask you all: if one has received the three groups of ten inexhaustible great precepts, yet commits any of the seven obstructing offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*), one should not proceed to receive them further.
I now ask you again: answer truthfully. If you do not answer truthfully, none of you shall obtain the precepts.
"O Bhikṣus, have you ever shed the blood of a Buddha? [They replied, "No. "Have you ever murdered your father? [They replied, "No. "Have you ever murdered your mother? [They replied, "No.
"Have you committed the act of murdering your preceptor (upādhyāya)? [They replied, "No. "Have you murdered your teacher (ācārya)? [They replied, "No.
"Have you disrupted the Saṃgha by breaking the *karmavācanā* or turning back the Wheel of Dharma? [They replied, "No. "Have you murdered..."
The Sage said, "No" (answering, "There are none"). If one is free from the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*), they are a truly pure vessel.

They may approach an Upādhyāya to request that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas bestow the Bodhisattva precepts. Since there are no grave transgressions before and no seven heinous offenses after, the precepts can be received.

[The assembly] harmonizes [in this way]: "Reflecting upon the various evil karmas created in the past, [one should contemplate] the extraordinary and superior practice of the merit of the precepts," and so forth.

The Sūtras and Vinaya state that regarding the ritual for the fortnightly *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts, there are thirty-six types of *poṣadha* ceremonies mentioned in the preceding section on precepts.

These include what are known as the *ānanda-poṣadha*, the *caura-poṣadha*, the *nau-poṣadha*, the *vana-poṣadha*, the *sāyāhna-poṣadha*, and the *pratyūṣa-poṣadha*. The World-Honored One did not permit any of these, as some were performed too late.
Or it may be too early. When monks from various regions arrive late for the assembly and the resident monks have already finished the *poṣadha*, these arriving monks are displeased.
They go to inform the World-Honored One, who addresses the monks, saying: "It is too early in the morning; wait for the monks to arrive.
Every half-month, at the time of noon, perform the *poṣadha*. Arrange high seats and offer incense and flowers as an offering. He permits this.
The junior monks each donned their five-, seven-, or nine-panel *kāṣāya* robes and, each holding a scroll of the Sūtras or Vinaya, went to where the Dharma Master was.
With single-minded attention they listened as the Upādhyāya or Ācārya expounded the teachings; if he were unable to do so, they would simply recite the ten heavy and forty-eight light precepts.
The fourfold assembly all proceeded to that place, with single-minded concentration and attentive ears, listening intently.
Therefore it is called *poṣadha*. When monks dwell together in harmony, this is also termed *poṣadha* and so forth;
it is not that the act of confessing offenses is what is called *poṣadha*, for such is an error.

Alternatively, even if there is no assembly and not even a single person is present, one may reverently face the Buddha and recite one fascicle by oneself; this is termed the "one-person *poṣadha*. This is performed every half-month. [Old...]

For those who have received the Bodhisattva precepts, on the day of the *poṣadha* for the examination of the precepts (*śīla-parīkṣā*), one should also follow the previous ritual procedure to invite the *ācārya* who is capable of performing the examination of the precepts through *karmavācanā*.
This may also be done in a secluded place; one must not examine the precepts in the presence of laypeople who do not possess the precepts.
If it is within a great assembly, the high seats shall be prepared by the members of the fourfold assembly and those who hold the full precepts, with incense and flowers arranged in rows.
Taking one's seat according to the Dharma (the invitation to come forward from the assembly):

"Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind. [I,] so-and-so, have been dispatched by the Master of this hall to extend an invitation for you, Venerable One, to serve as the Preceptor for Examining the Precepts (*śīla-vicaya-ācārya*) for this assembly.
By relying upon you, Venerable One, we shall be able to perform the rite of repentance. Out of compassion, please grant us your favor."
Out of compassion. Out of great compassion. (Striking the sounding block).
O sons of the Buddha, since you have so earnestly extended this request, I shall act as your *śīlācārya* (preceptor for the examination of precepts) for your sakes.
Listen with single-minded attention to all these teachings. O Sons of the Buddha, as the half-month has passed, you should perform the *poṣadha* rite.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *poṣadha*, which here means "I confess. Facing one another, each shall personally declare the nature of the transgressions they have committed;
no faults may be concealed. One must repent according to the Dharma. Through repentance there is peace and happiness; without repentance, there is only sin.

[The Master] says, "Profound. First, he calls those who have received the five precepts and the eight precepts to come forward; once they have finished confessing their transgressions, he dismisses them.
Next, he calls those who have received the ten precepts and the śrāmaṇeras to come forward; once they have finished confessing their transgressions, he dismisses them.
Again, call the bhikṣus to leave their seats and confess. Examine whether they have committed any transgression among the two hundred and fifty precepts.

If there is none, let them remain silent; because they are pure, this matter is thus maintained. Have them depart, and only then examine the characteristics of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of the bodhisattva.
According to their gravity or lightness, do not treat a grave offense as light, nor a light one as grave.

The commission of offenses is grave. To establish what was not prescribed as prescribed, or to violate what has been prescribed—should one fail to examine the precepts in this manner, one incurs guilt.
Examine the ten categories of *pārājika* offenses.
Venerable sirs, if there be any who have committed an offense, each must disclose it; you must not conceal it.
First, the precept against killing (Have you committed this? Answer: No). Second, the precept against stealing (Have you committed this? Answer: No).
Third, the precept against sexual misconduct (If you have, say so; if not, say no). Fourth, the precept against false speech (Have you committed this? Answer: No).
The fifth precept: selling intoxicants (the following items are as before). The sixth precept: speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly.
The seventh precept: praising oneself and disparaging others. The eighth precept: being stingy and resentful while further disparaging others.
The ninth precept: refusing to accept an apology out of anger. The tenth precept: slandering the Triple Gem.

If one has committed a grave offense, they shall be made to repent until an auspicious sign is seen; if there is no offense, it is because the assembly is pure. One should maintain this matter in this way.
These are the forty-eight minor transgressions.

Venerable sirs, if there are those who have committed minor offenses (light impurities), they should confess each one before the Three Jewels and the great assembly, declaring their transgressions face-to-face with another;
thus they shall be extinguished. This is not like the ten grave offenses, which require the seeking of auspicious signs.
First, the precept against disrespecting teachers and friends (answer regarding transgression: none). Second, the precept against drinking alcohol (the following are identical to the preceding).
Third, the precept against eating meat. Fourth, the precept against eating the five pungent roots.
Fifth, the precept against failing to instruct others on repentance for their offenses. Sixth, the precept against failing to provide offerings when requested to teach the Dharma.
Seventh, the precept against laziness and failing to listen to the Dharma; eighth, the precept against turning away from the Great Vehicle and inclining toward the Small Vehicle;
ninth, the precept against failing to tend to the sick; tenth, the precept against keeping implements for killing;
eleventh, the precept regarding acting as a government envoy; twelfth, the precept against engaging in trade and commerce.

Venerable sirs, if there is anyone among you who has committed an offense, please come forward and confess it. If you have not committed an offense, remain silent; by your silence, we shall know that you are pure in this matter.
Thus, let this be held as such.
When the Buddha was in the world, he was constantly followed by a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
They resided in the mountains, each practicing different paths, upholding heterodox views, prohibitions, and ascetic mortifications—methods that were not ultimate.
These included fifty companions of the elder’s son Yaśas, five hundred disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, and two hundred disciples of Nadī-Kāśyapa.
There were one hundred and fifty people; Kāśyapa of Gayā and his disciples numbered two hundred and fifty;
Śāriputra and his disciples numbered one hundred; and Mahāmaudgalyāyana and his disciples numbered one hundred.

These one thousand two hundred and fifty individuals had all previously served non-Buddhist teachers, undergoing arduous asceticism for many kalpas without attaining any realization. Having received the Buddha’s transformative guidance, they each received full ordination.

He immediately attained the realization of the fruit. Thereupon, moved by the Buddha’s grace, he traveled far and wide; at every Dharma assembly, he constantly followed the Buddha without ever leaving him.

Thus, it is of such individuals that the opening sections of various sutras speak when they list "the one thousand two hundred and fifty people who were well-known to all" as being present with the Buddha.

Robes: fifth, the childbirth robe. These five kinds of impure robes should not be kept. The rain-bath robe and the wound-covering robe should be kept.

The four dharmas of *karma* are: first, the dharma; second, the matter; third, the persons; fourth, the boundary.
Regarding the four types of alms-food for the *dhūta* practitioner: begging for food, not making "leftover food," eating in a single sitting, and taking a single portion of solid food in one vessel.

The four categories of dhūta garments consist of two types: the patched robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and the three robes (*tricīvara*). Regarding food: alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*), eating at a single sitting (*ekāsana*), and so forth. Regarding place:
the forest hermitage (*araṇya*), among tombs (*śmāśānika*), and at the foot of a tree (*vṛkṣamūlika*). Regarding posture: always sitting (*naiṣadyika*). There is no fixed order to these.
By begging for alms, one brings benefit and welfare to all living beings, subdues arrogance, recognizes that the body is subject to attachment,
and eliminates lingering attachments— the four root afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, and pride.
The Vinaya has four meanings: first, it is the level ground within the Buddha-dharma, from which all myriad virtues arise;

second, all initial disciples of the Buddha abide by relying upon the precepts, and the entire assembly exists by depending on the precepts; third, it is the primary gateway for proceeding toward Nirvana;
and fourth, it is the jeweled necklace of the Buddha-dharma, for it is able to adorn the Buddha-dharma.

There are four conditions for relinquishing the precepts, whereby one abandons what has been studied and thus relinquishes the precepts: (1) the arising of both sexual organs; (2) the transformation from female to male or from male to female;
(3) the severing of the roots of goodness, the undertaking of unwholesome precepts, or the adoption of wrong views; and (4) the relinquishing of the commonality of the group or the death of the body.

The four meanings of *śīla* are: the meaning of "coolness," because it removes the feverish afflictions of the mind; the meaning of "security," because it serves as the cause for happiness in future lives;
the meaning of "tranquility," because it can establish *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; and the meaning of "extinction," because it is the cause for attaining *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding the four precepts for collecting the mind, first sever sexual desire of the mind. Even a slight attachment in the mind is the root of lust. Next, sever killing of the mind;
mental anger constitutes killing, which leads one into the realm of spirits. Third, sever theft of the mind; to be deceitful, secretive, and perverse out of greed, and not to relinquish it, is theft.
Fourth, sever false speech; to claim for oneself that one has attained the Dharma of a sage is called falsehood.
Having accomplished the four dharmas of dignified deportment, one knows that the three realms of existence are not defiled and that they are suffering.
My own suffering and joy are the same as those of others; I constantly practice patience—neither being arrogant when above nor feeling ashamed when below.
By practicing humility, one attains four kinds of merit: one remains far removed from the evil destinies and is not reborn as an animal; one is not subjected to contempt or disparagement;
one is always honored by humans and devas; and malicious friends and enemies cannot assail or overcome one.
When Bodhisattvas practice these four dharmas, they skillfully discern that which is manifested from their own minds; they contemplate external natures as being neither existent nor non-existent;
they depart from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing; and they attain the sublime joy of the noble wisdom of self-realization.

The fourfold meaning of a bhikṣu’s possession of the precepts comprises: first, formal ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), which refers to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the ritual procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations);
second, subsequent possession, which refers to the constant maintenance and concealment of the two types of precepts from that point onward;

third, possession through protecting the minds of others, which refers to the partial perfection of a bhikṣu’s dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) called "protecting the minds of others"; and fourth, possession through guarding the precepts.
This means that one perceives fear in even minor transgressions and does not commit them; should one commit them, one must confess them.

The Bodhisattva has four wheels: being born in a central land (the wheel of birth in a central land destroys the difficulties of the three evil realms, the northern continent, and the long-lived heavens);

cultivating the wheel of right aspiration (which destroys the difficulty of worldly wisdom and cleverness); and planting the wheel of goodness (which destroys the difficulties of blindness, deafness, and muteness).
Overcoming the difficulty of being mute; approaching virtuous persons; overcoming the difficulties regarding what was taught before and after the Buddha;

dividing the alms-food into four parts: one part to offer to fellow practitioners of the holy life, one to give to destitute beggars, one to give to various spirits and deities, and one part to eat oneself.
One should practice four dharmas: rather than losing one's body or life, never abandon the bodhicitta; draw near to virtuous friends; never abandon patience; and rely on secluded places.

Regarding the observance of precepts, there are four types: the precept of fearing the four terrors; the precept of not seeking ill repute or punishment; the precept of aspiration; and the precept of not coveting wealth or fame.

The *śīla* of renown and so forth; the *śīla* of conforming to awakening; the *śīla* of seeking the fruit of liberation and so forth, which is pure; and the untainted (*anāsrava*) *śīla* that is free from afflictions and so forth.

Regarding the four categories of lay followers (*upāsaka*): those who possess no portion merely receive the three refuges; those with a small portion receive one precept; those with a large portion receive two, three, or four;
and those with a full portion receive all five precepts in their entirety.
The four kinds of Dharma for the mastery of Bodhisattvas as śramaṇas are: first, precepts; second, supernormal powers; third, knowledge; and fourth, wisdom.

The four mentalities with which a disciple regards their preceptor are: first, regarding the teacher as a beloved parent; second, regarding the teacher with respectful compliance; and third, regarding the teacher with a sense of awe and dread.
There are four types of venerable masters.

Regarding the three levels of birth based on the degree of keeping the precepts: those who break the precepts are born as animals, hungry ghosts, or in hell; those who maintain the precepts to a lower degree are born in the human realm;

and those who maintain the precepts to a middle degree are born among the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm. Furthermore, they may also practice the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments.
Concentration. Those born in the realms of form and formlessness; those who uphold the precepts in the highest degree, Arhats in the middle, and Pratyekabuddhas in the lower;

and the path of the Buddha in the highest. There are four kinds of heavy debts of gratitude: parents, because they gave one physical birth, must be repaid; the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher; and the teacher who expounds the Dharma.
There are four kinds of bhikṣus: the bhikṣu who has ultimately reached the Path, namely the Arhat, also called one who has attained the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);
the bhikṣu who demonstrates the Path, namely the noble ones of the three [upper] fruits, also called those in the first, second, or third fruits;

the bhikṣu who receives the Path, namely those in the stage of approaching the first fruit, also called those who have passed through the stages of both the outer and inner ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); and the bhikṣu who defiles the Path, namely the ordinary person who breaks the precepts, also called one who commits the four [grave offenses].
As for the significant points:
the Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, attained enlightenment in Magadha, preached the Dharma in Vārāṇasī,
and entered parinirvāṇa in Kuśinagara.
The four root afflictions: the affliction of greed, the affliction of hatred, the affliction of delusion, and the affliction of pride.
The five kinds of turning away from heterodoxy: the five precepts, the eight precepts, the ten precepts, and the full precepts.
The five colors of the *kāṣāya* are: vermilion (red), green (copper-green), black (mixed clay), madder (tree bark), and purple.
The five kinds of repentance do not necessarily require prostrations. One should constantly contemplate the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

One should filially support one’s parents, revere teachers and elders, govern the state according to the True Dharma, and not oppress the people. On the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*), one should issue a decree throughout the realm to prohibit killing.
One should have deep faith in cause and effect and know that the Buddha does not perish.
1. Not responding to invitations and remaining at ease; 2. The devas preaching the Dharma; 3. Observing the sick; 4.
Guarding over bedding and requisites; 5. The training rules of the precepts.
Five factors that assist the precepts: faith, shame, dread of blame, virtuous friends, and revering the precepts. Receiving the worldly precepts and honoring the Buddha.

The Precepts: By observing the five precepts, one is reborn in the heavens. By refraining from killing, one is reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*). By refraining from stealing, one is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. By refraining from sexual misconduct, one is reborn in the Yāma Heaven.
By refraining from false speech, one is reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. By refraining from drinking alcohol and eating meat, one is reborn in the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmitavaśavartin Heavens.
O Deva. There are five kinds of ācāryas upon whom one relies to obtain ordination: the *karmavācanā* master who bestows the precepts and performs the ritual;
the instructor who teaches the proper deportment; the master of the scriptures who transmits the four-line verses and so forth; and the *upādhyāya* (preceptor).
Shangxue, having observed the precepts for ten summer retreats (*daśavarṣa*), acted as a teacher to others.
Regarding the five types of water-strainers (*parisrāvaṇa*): the *fangluo* (square strainer) uses three feet of silk to form a one-foot square; its size may be adjusted according to the occasion.
The *faping* (dharma-flask) and *yin yangping* (yin-yang flask). The *junchi* (military-strainer): the mouth is tied with silk, and it is suspended by a rope in the water; once full, it is drawn out.

The water-strainer for drawing water: one should simply take a square piece of fine silk measuring one *tāla* (a fathom) and tie it over the mouth of the jar; or use a corner of one’s robe as a strainer to filter water into the bowl.
One should not ask questions for the sake of testing others, nor out of doubt, nor for the purpose of repenting for transgressions committed.
One asks because of what has been received; one asks because of the difficulty of the discourse.
Regarding the five dharmas of leaving home: one leaves home having resolved upon it, cherishing the Holy Path within. One alters one’s physical appearance and should don the Dharma robes.
One casts aside body and life to honor the Way of the Dharma. One forever severs affection for kin, neither favoring nor rejecting anyone. One aspires to seek [the truth].
The Mahāyāna is for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
A bhikṣu possesses five qualities that terrify Māra: he is a mendicant, pure in his precepts, pure in his livelihood, and a destroyer of evil.

One who breaks the precepts suffers five decays: he fails to obtain wealth when seeking it; even if he obtains it, it is squandered; the assembly does not love or respect him; and an evil reputation spreads abroad.
If one dies [having violated them], they will enter hell.

There are five faults in breaking the precepts that bring harm to oneself: being censured by the wise, a bad reputation spreading abroad, regretting only at the time of death, and entering the evil realms after death.

The five benefits of the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka) are most peaceful and secure: the mind is not distracted; it is a defense against the King of Māras; one has no fear of non-Buddhists (tīrthika); the mind is easily stilled;
and the bhikṣu’s five virtues possess a nature of pliancy. This is a metaphor for how those who have left the household life can subdue the coarseness of body and speech.
The spreading of trailing vines on all sides is a metaphor for how those who have left the household life transmit the Dharma and deliver sentient beings in an unbroken succession.
The fragrance being perceived from afar is a metaphor for how the precepts and virtues of those who have left the household life are so fragrant that they reach everyone’s ears.

Its ability to cure pain is a metaphor for how those who have left the household life can sever the poisonous harm of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Not turning one's back to the sun is a metaphor for how those who have left the household life always face toward the Buddha.
Daytime sleep has five faults: bad dreams, lack of protection by the devas, the mind not entering the Dharma, failure to contemplate the signs of light,
and the emission of semen.
The five benefits of the *yānjī* (teeth-cleansing twig) are: first, it prevents the mouth from smelling foul; second, it provides a pleasant flavor to the mouth and prevents a bitter taste;

third, it removes heat; fourth, it can eliminate wind-disorders and dispel wind; fifth, it also removes obstructions and aids digestion, while eliminating phlegm and mucus; furthermore, it clarifies the eyesight.
Chewing [food] improperly has five faults: the breath becomes foul, one cannot distinguish flavors, phlegm is not digested, it does not stimulate the appetite, and the eyes lose their clarity.

There are five matters regarding circumambulation (when a bhikṣu has prostrated before the Buddha, he must circumambulate to the right and not turn to the left, just as the sun, moon, and stars revolve around Mount Sumeru): keep one's head bowed and gaze at the ground.
One must not step on insects. One must not look left or right. One must not spit on the ground. One must not converse with others. By circumambulating [the stupa], one obtains five blessings:
in future lives, one will obtain an upright and handsome appearance; one will obtain a beautiful voice; one will be reborn in the heavens;
one will be born into the family of kings or nobles; and one will attain the Way of Nirvana.
When begging for alms, one must avoid five types of households: those that shout out their wares, those of the *caṇḍālas*, taverns, government offices, and brothels.

When entering the houses of laypeople, one should observe five practices upon entering the door: speak softly, restrain body, speech, and mind, humble one’s posture, and well-guard the sense faculties.
Dignified deportment and orderly conduct inspire goodness in others.
There are five places where one should not frequent: the residence of government officials, taverns, butcher shops, and brothels.
According to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, there are: first, the *pārājika* rules; second, the *bhikṣuṇī-pārājika* rules; and third, the robes for receiving the precepts.

The *Bhaiṣajyavastu*, the *Āhāravastu*, and so forth; the four methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*); the five rules concerning schism in the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*) and miscellaneous matters (*kṣudraka-vastu*).
Regarding the five categories of offenses, there are two hundred and fifty articles for Bhikṣus and three hundred and forty-eight articles for Bhikṣuṇīs; at present, only forty-one remain.
As for the "articles," by adding the two *aniyata* (undetermined) rules and the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (methods for settling disputes), they total fifty articles.
Furthermore, within the number seven, one observes the seven groups and six groups.
Regarding the five methods of repentance: bare the right shoulder, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms with a sincere heart, and bow the head in salutation.
This is sufficient. To state the names of the offenses:
one who upholds the Vinaya attains five merits: their precepts become firm; they are well able to overcome all adversaries; they are fearless in making definitive judgments within the assembly;
they are able to resolve the doubts and regrets of others; and by skillfully upholding the precepts, they cause the True Dharma to endure for a long time.
During the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one must avoid five faults: being too far from a village so that requisites are difficult to obtain;
being too near a city so as to obstruct the practice of the path; having many mosquitoes and ants that bite and sting or trample and injure living beings;
lacking a person upon whom one can rely—one who possesses the five virtues may be relied upon; and lacking a donor to provide food, drink, and medicinal decoctions.

The Bodhisattva’s giving is endowed with four mental states: knowing the true nature of giving such that the three spheres are all empty; giving rise to a mind of compassion to uproot suffering and bestow happiness;
making the vow to attain the unsurpassed fruit; and dedicating and transferring the merit throughout the Dharma-realm. Possessing skillful means, they cultivate all various practices to fulfillment.

The five precepts correspond to the five aggregates (*skandha*): non-killing corresponds to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); non-stealing corresponds to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); non-sexual misconduct corresponds to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*);
non-lying corresponds to the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and abstaining from alcohol and meat corresponds to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Violating the five precepts leads to being oppressed by the five stars and the destruction of the precepts. Now, one is oppressed by Jupiter, resulting in the premature loss of life and limb.

Violating the precept against stealing leads to poverty and low status; now, one is oppressed by Venus, resulting in destitution and base birth. Violating the precept against sexual misconduct leads to the imposition of royal punishment;

now, one is oppressed by Mars, resulting in legal penalties. Violating the precept against false speech leads to one’s words being disbelieved; now, one is oppressed by Saturn, resulting in untrustworthy speech. Violating the precept against intoxicants...
Now, alcohol is oppressed by the planet Mercury; it is the deafening obstruction of ignorance.

Even those who have entered my Dharma through the five kinds of merits of the *kāṣāya*, yet commit grave offenses, hold false views, and so forth—even for a single thought-moment—[are affected by this].
One who respects it with a reverent heart will certainly receive a prediction of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles.
If devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits can show even a small measure of reverence toward this *kāṣāya*, they shall immediately attain non-retrogression in the Three Vehicles.

If there are ghosts, spirits, or humans who obtain even four inches of the *kāṣāya*, their food and drink will become sufficient. If there are sentient beings who are at odds with one another, by recollecting the power of the *kāṣāya*, [they shall be reconciled].
He immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness. If one upholds even a small portion of this [teaching], honoring and respecting it, one will always prevail over others.
Even if a dragon wears but a single thread of it, they shall all be spared from the perils of the garuḍas.

Regarding the dharma of dependence for five years: after five years have passed, one who knows five matters—namely, knowing the gravity of transgressions and knowing the *karmavācanā*—is called an *ācārya*.

Regarding the status of dependence for ten years: even if one does not know the *vinaya*, one must remain dependent on the *upādhyāya* for as long as life lasts; however, one who is thoroughly proficient in the *Śīlaskandha-piṭaka* [may act as an *upādhyāya*].
To act as a teacher for others and bestow the precepts upon them, yet do so otherwise [than correctly], one incurs immeasurable sin. One who lacks understanding cannot be a teacher.
The *Five Hundred Questions* states: "One should seek repentance; if one does not repent, the sin increases daily, and the recipient of the precepts will not obtain them."
Receiving the Bodhisattva precepts yields five kinds of benefits: first, the Buddhas of the ten directions take pity on one and constantly protect them;
second, at the time of death, one possesses right view and the mind is joyful; third, in every place of rebirth, one becomes a friend to all bodhisattvas.
Fourth, the perfection of the aggregate of merit through the precepts. Fifth, the fulfillment of the nature-precepts, merit, and wisdom in this and future lives.
The five categories of offenses correspond to the five punishments, the five elements, and the five *pārājikas*: [the first] is death; earth; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; flowing water.
Three *pāyattika* offenses: seizing gold; four *pratideśanīya* offenses: the staff, fire; five *dukkaṭa* offenses: the cane, wood.
[These correspond to] the five ancient punishments: branding, cutting the nose, cutting the feet, castration, and capital punishment.

By not eating after midday, one obtains five kinds of benefits: little sexual desire, little sleep, attainment of single-mindedness, absence of downward-moving wind (flatus), and physical ease without illness.

If one passes midday and puts even a morsel of salt or a drop of vinegar into the mouth, one falls into the Hell of the Scorched Intestines, except during times of illness, when giving robes, when making robes, when traveling far, or when performing [pilgrimage].
At the time of traveling by boat, at the time of a great assembly, at the time of giving food, and at the time of performing labor, it is permitted to eat while wearing the eight-strip robe;
there is no offense. There are five reasons why a *mahābhikṣu* may engage in such activities: to repay the Buddha’s grace; because the Vinaya permits a *bhikṣu* to personally manage a vihāra;
to nurture the Buddha-dharma; to eliminate the arrogance of inferior and common folk; and for the sake of future disciples.
Because it subdues arrogance and pride; because it initiates future meritorious karma;

and because the five precepts correspond to the ten wholesome paths of action, while the Saṃgha’s sixfold harmonies consist of harmony in precepts through collective practice, harmony in views through shared understanding, harmony in person through dwelling together, and harmony in material benefits through sharing.
Equanimity. Harmony of speech without contention; harmony of mind with shared joy.

For śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus, there are the six requisites (*ṣaḍ-vastu*)—one who lacks these six is called a "bald man"—and the six classes of offenses (*ṣaṭ-nikāya*), which in Indic are called *pārājika* (translated here as "abandonment"). In the Hīnayāna, these are said to be non-repentable; in the Mahāyāna, it is said:

*Pārājika*: This refers to the "defeats. *Saṃghāvaśeṣa*: This is translated as "residual offenses of the Saṃgha"; it is like severing a person's head, yet because the windpipe remains, [the life-force persists].
*Thullaccaya*: This is translated as "grave offense" or "ugly offense. *Pāyattika*: This is translated as "falling.

Because one has committed an offense involving forfeiture due to handling wealth, and has not yet performed confession, it is called *pāyattika*. *Pratideśanīya*: This is translated as "to be confessed. *Duṣkṛta*: This is translated as...

"Evil conduct and evil speech. To the six categories [of offenses], "evil speech" is added to form seven categories. Regarding the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), the Chinese term is "huá" (flower) and the Sanskrit is "puṣpa.

As for the seven classes of practitioners, the *bhikṣu* is called a "beggar" (*yācanaka*) because he maintains a pure livelihood; he is also named such because he is able to destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore...

It is called "Able to Terrify Māra. Regarding the term *bhikṣuṇī*: *nī* means woman. Because the Buddha considered the monastic regulations (*vinaya*) to be inconvenient for women, he placed them after the *śramaṇas*.
When his maternal aunt requested ordination, he did not grant it; only after she practiced the Eight Respectful Rules (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) did he permit it.
*Śikṣamāṇā* is translated here as "nun training in the precepts. An eighteen-year-old girl should train in the precepts for two years to discipline her body and mind, and to know what exists...
"Womb" and "non-womb" refer to the three fundamental dharmas and the six dharmas of practice. *Śrāmaṇera*:
this is translated as "one who rests from evil and practices kindness," meaning to cease harmful conduct and cultivate compassion. It is also rendered as "Diligent Encourager Male. *Śrāmaṇerī*:

this is translated as "Diligent Encourager Female. *Upāsaka*: the meaning is translated as "Faithful Layman Male"; he is also called "Virtuous Layman Male," "Pure Layman," or "Pure Layman Male. Furthermore, [he is also called]...

The *upāsaka* (lay male devotee) and the *upāsikā* (lay female devotee)—the meanings of which are "faithful man" and "faithful woman," and are also called "virtuous man" and "virtuous woman"—though both remain householders, are able to observe the five precepts; men and women reside in separate quarters.

The sevenfold precepts consist of abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct (the three of body); and abstaining from false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech (the four of speech). These actions performed by body and speech are termed "karma";
when each is prefixed with the character for "not" (*a-*), they are termed "precepts."
One who upholds the Vinaya attains seven merits: they are able to uphold the Buddha’s inner treasury; they are able to skillfully resolve disputes; they maintain the precepts;
because of the Vinaya, non-Buddhists remain bowed in reverence before them; they have no need to consult others when reciting the Prātimokṣa before the assembly, for they are fearless;
they are able to sever doubt; and they are able to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time.

In the *Dharmayuan* (Garden of Dharma), there are seven cases of conception through physical contact. In one instance, a man touched a woman’s body with his own, immediately giving rise to lustful attachment and thereby conceiving a fetus.
Udāyin took his robe and went forth with his wife; his desire did not cease, and his semen stained the garment. A nun licked the garment and conceived a fetus.
[In another case], semen was discharged, and a female deer smelled the ascetic’s semen; driven by lustful intent, she drank it and consequently became pregnant.
Conception through touch: the parents of the Bodhisattva were both blind; they left the household life to practice the Way and did not engage in sexual union.
Because of [the mother’s] touch with her hand, she conceived a child upon merely looking at a man. Conception through sound: the female egrets are all female and have no males;
when spring arrives, they conceive upon hearing the sound of thunder. Conception through smell: a *qín* cow conceives as soon as it smells the scent of its calf.

The seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya-karma*) are: killing one's father; killing one's mother; killing one's *upādhyāya*; killing one's *ācārya*; causing a schism in the *saṃgha* (the breaking of the *karmavācanā*);
killing a noble being of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi-ārya*); and shedding the blood of a Buddha.
Regarding the seven methods for settling disputes: where the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) should be applied, one should apply the *sammukhā-vinaya*;

where the *smṛti-vinaya* (settlement by recollection) should be applied, one should apply the *smṛti-vinaya*; where the *amūḷha-vinaya* (settlement for one no longer insane) should be applied, one should apply the *amūḷha-vinaya*;

where the *pratijñā-kāraka* (settlement by confession) should be applied, one should apply the *pratijñā-kāraka*; where the *tassapāpiyasika* (settlement for a more serious offense) should be applied, one should apply the *tassapāpiyasika*.
One should grant the *tassapāpiyasikā* (formal act for one who repeatedly seeks out faults); one ought to grant the *tassapāpiyasikā*; one shall grant the *tassapāpiyasikā*.
One should grant the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass); one ought to grant the *tiṇavatthāraka*; one shall grant the *tiṇavatthāraka*.

Venerable sirs, these seven principles for the settlement of disputes are recited every half-month from within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. Whenever a legal issue arises among the bhikṣus, it should be settled immediately.

An upāsaka possesses eight qualities: faith, ethical discipline, generosity, listening to the Dharma, receiving and upholding it, understanding its meaning, practicing according to the teaching, and the eight awakenings of a great person—
fewness of desires, contentment, tranquility, diligence, right mindfulness, right concentration, right wisdom, and freedom from conceptual proliferation.
The eight dharmas of a bodhisattva are: first, not speaking of the faults of others even at the cost of one’s life; second, transforming people so that they take refuge in the Triple Gem;
third, establishing all beings in the bodhicitta; fourth, remaining untainted by the brahma-conduct; fifth, fashioning images of the Buddha and placing them upon flowered pedestals;
sixth, being able to remove the grief and affliction of sentient beings; and seventh, always regarding those who are arrogant with humility.

Being humble and modest; eighth, not vexing others. The *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva accomplishes eight dharmas, they will be born by transformation upon a lotus flower in the presence of all Buddhas."

One should revere the *kāṣāya* with the eight dharmas: one should conceive of it as a stūpa; one should conceive of it as quiescence (*śānti*); one should conceive of it as loving-kindness (*maitrī*); one should conceive of it as compassion (*karuṇā*);
one should conceive of it as the Buddha; one should conceive of it as shame (*hrī*); and one should conceive of it as remorse (*apatrāpya*). One should think:
"May I, in future lives, be free from the three poisons and become a true śramaṇa. As the Sūtra says: "The *kāṣāya* is the insignia of the noble ones. Following [this principle]...

Regarding *kārttika*, the *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā* states that for the sake of brevity, it is simply called *kārttika*. This translates as "merit" (*guṇa*). Because...

To have merit in observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is to receive the reward of five benefits. According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), *kārttika* is translated as the Pleiades (*mǎo xīng*).
Because the Pleiades constellation governs this month, the *Lüchão* (Vinaya Commentary) cites the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Vibhāṣā*) to translate it as "solid" (*jiānshí*).

It is so called because it can induce solid results and the acquisition of many robes, for one's clothing will not be ruined. It is also named "difficult to sustain" (*nánhuó*), because for a greedy person, sustaining life is difficult; yet by giving up a little [of one's possessions], one finds it easy.
When wealth enters this robe, its merit is superior; it is as if one were giving a great mass of robes as large as Mount Sumeru. It is also called "firm" (*kaṭhina*) or "sheltering" (*channa*).

In ancient translations, it was rendered as the "robe for rewarding the good and punishing the evil," because it rewards those who completed the *pūrvavāra* (first half) of the rainy season retreat (whereas those who joined later or those who did not practice the retreat do not receive it).
It is also translated as the "robe of merit" (*guṇa-kaṭhina*), because when the Saṃgha collectively receives this robe, they attract five kinds of beneficial merits. [As stated] in the Vinaya:

Because of receiving this robe, one may keep extra wealth, stay overnight apart from one's robes, and all [types of] invitations, including eating in a group separate from the community (*pṛthag-bhaktika*) and visiting other households before or after meals.

Those who entered the retreat early shall receive it on the sixteenth day of the seventh month and relinquish it on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* further states: "If one obtains a new robe..."
Regarding robes offered by a donor or *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) clothing, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states: A *pāṃśukūla* is not the clothing of a dead person. New material is purified by folding it;

if it has already been washed, it is purified by folding it after washing. It must be received on the same day and not kept overnight. One must not obtain it through the decline of one's life-force; it must be in accordance with the Dharma.
It should have borders on all four sides, consist of five strips with ten sections, and be the color of a *kāṣāya*. Its acceptance and relinquishment should be performed accordingly.
